worksheet.title: Loop a Pattern in Code
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.1 — repeating events
worksheet.learning_goal: I can loop a small pattern of moves to make a staircase.

parts.title: Repeat a little pattern
text: A staircase is the same step over and over. Bit's step is: go across, then go up. A loop repeats that step to build the whole staircase.
Read the code — range(3) repeats the across-then-up step three times.

parts.title: Read this Python code
parts.code:
for step in range(3):
    bit.forward(30)
    bit.left(90)
    bit.forward(30)
    bit.right(90)

parts.caption: Each repeat is one step: across, then up. range(3) makes 3 steps.

parts.title: Read it
parts.prompt: How many steps does the staircase have? ______  Each step has 2 forward moves, so how many forward moves in TOTAL? ______

parts.title: Predict, then run
parts.prompt: You change range(3) to range(5). PREDICT: how many steps, and how many forward moves in total? Then run it.

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Make Bit climb a 4-step staircase. Write the range number:  for step in range(______):

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Each step goes UP 30. If Bit climbs a 4-step staircase, how high does Bit go in total? Show your thinking.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A loop can repeat a little PATTERN of moves, not just one move. Repeat the across-then-up step and Bit builds a whole staircase.

teacher_guide.title: Loop a Pattern in Code
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: A staircase is the same little step over and over: go across, then go up. Students read a repeat that does that whole step several times to build a staircase, and count the moves and total height. A repeat can repeat a whole pattern, not just one move. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start — showing the drawing (optional)
text: The worksheet shows the typed instructions AND a picture of the staircase Bit climbs, so you can teach straight from the printout — no computer required.

To show it live (optional): open a browser, go to a free "Python turtle" playground (e.g. search "trinket python turtle"), type the few lines from the worksheet, and press Run — a turtle draws it. You only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Walk a staircase as a class — across, up, across, up — and name the repeating step.
2. Show it (you do). Run the 3-step staircase; trace one step, then the repeat. Graph paper helps students sketch it.
3. Let them work. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 multiplies the rise), solo or in pairs.
4. Wrap up: a repeat can repeat a whole pattern of moves, not just one.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — 3 steps; 6 forward moves (2 per step × 3).
Exercise 2 — 5 steps; 10 forward moves in total.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: counting one forward per step instead of two.
Make it easier: highlight the two "move forward" lines inside the repeat before counting.
Make it harder: ask the height of a 6-step staircase (180).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The student counts steps and total forwards (Ex 1–2), writes the repeat number for a 4-step staircase (Ex 3), and multiplies to find the total height (Ex 4).
